name: Grand Palace
label: Grand Palace
camera_pill: near สนามราชกิจ
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23482754: large area 'Grand Palace' (805 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Former royal residence with ornate halls and spires.

text.description:
The Grand Palace is not one building but a walled complex of halls, pavilions, courtyards and lawns on the bank of the Chao Phraya River. Work began on 6 May 1782, when King Rama I moved the capital across the river from Thonburi to Bangkok. Later kings kept adding to it, so the styles are mixed and the layout is irregular. The whole site covers about 218,400 square metres and is divided into several quarters, including the Temple of the Emerald Buddha and the Outer, Middle and Inner Courts. It is still a working royal palace, and more than eight million people visit each year.

That variety is what makes it rewarding on a phone. Look for the walls, rooftops and spires of the palace, which make a strong, simple picture. Closer in, you can switch to close-up shots of rooflines, gables and decoration. The site is so large that one spot cannot show everything, so treat this as your wide establishing shot and then move closer.

Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the full sweep of wall and rooftops, and the telephoto lens for details. Keep your phone level, since the straight walls and tall spires look odd when tilted. Expect other visitors in the frame, and use them to show the scale if you like.
text.geographic_location: In the Phra Nakhon District, on Rattanakosin Island, beside the Chao Phraya River in the old heart of Bangkok. Sanam Luang lies to the north and Wat Pho is just to the south.
text.directions_text: Head for Rattanakosin Island in Phra Nakhon District, in the old part of Bangkok, and ask for the Grand Palace. Once there, walk to the phone icon on the map. From it the palace is 112 m to the north-east, about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in the length of the wall and the rooftops behind it. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out roofs, spires and decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Move a few steps sideways if people or vehicles block the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the walls up with the horizontal grid lines so they stay straight. Leave a band of sky above the roofs and spires so they are not cropped. Use telephoto for a tighter second shot of a single roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest roof or wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little. Bright sky and pale walls can fool the phone into making the scene too light or too dark. Check the corners of ultra-wide shots for stretched people or poles.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the site is quieter and the light is softer. Midday sun is harsh and the light bounces off pale surfaces, so check your shots on screen.

text.access_note: The palace is partly open to the public as a museum but is still a working royal palace, so check the official site before you go for access and dress rules.

name: Wat Arun
label: Wat Arun
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tha Tien' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Home Cafe Tha Tien' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23481741: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Arun' (387 m across).
notes: Temple of Dawn with its tall prang on the Chao Phraya River.

text.description:
Wat Arun, the Temple of Dawn, is the tall, pale prang that rises over the western bank of the Chao Phraya River. The temple has been here since at least the 17th century, but the prang you see today dates from the early 19th century. It was finished in 1851 after about nine years of building. Its height is often given as anywhere between roughly 67 and 86 metres. Up close, the surface is covered in bits of porcelain and shell. Four smaller prang stand at its corners. A big restoration between 2013 and 2017 gave it the brighter, whiter look it has now.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear and the river gives you open space around it. The best-known view is from Tha Tien on the opposite bank. From there the whole prang sits across the water, and at sunset the sun can fall behind or beside it, with its reflection in the river. Guides describe this as the classic postcard angle, and it is a free public walkway. The late-afternoon crowd gathers there, so arrive about 30 minutes before sunset to find a spot. Two alternatives are a riverside point reached by a lane off Maha Rat Road, and the temple grounds themselves, where you can fill the frame with the prang or take a full-length shot of a friend in front of it.
text.geographic_location: Wat Arun is in Bangkok Yai district, in Thonburi on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River. The recommended viewpoint, Tha Tien, is on the east bank, across the river and to the north-east of the temple.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops listed near this spot, so head for Tha Tien pier on the east bank, a short walk from the Wat Pho pier area. Once at the riverside, walk to the open space in front of the pier and look west across the water. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole prang, the river and the sky in one frame. Use 2x or more only if you want a tighter shot of the spire and its decoration. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for wide scenes with lots of sky, as the temple will look small in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Tha Tien (east bank, riverside in front of the pier, facing west across the Chao Phraya; stand clear of the ferry gangway). The whole white prang across the river, with the sun setting behind or beside it and its reflection in the water. Keep clear of the ferry gangway so you do not block passengers.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the prang on one of the vertical lines, with the river filling the lower third so the reflection shows. Wait for a gap in the crowd and keep the phone level so the spire stays upright. If you want a different angle, try the lane viewpoint off Maha Rat Road for a view of the central prang rising above the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky near the prang to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sunset colours stay rich and the temple does not turn into a flat silhouette. After the floodlights come on, switch to night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or wall to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About 30 to 40 minutes before sunset for golden light, then stay for the blue hour once the floodlights come on. Sunset times change through the year, so check the time for your date. One guide says the sun sets almost directly behind the prang from mid-February to mid-March.

text.access_note: The riverside at Tha Tien is a public walkway, but Wat Arun itself has entry rules, fees and a dress code, so check the official site before you go.

name: Khaosan Road
label: Khao San Road
camera_pill: near ถนนข้าวสาร
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1516377328: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Khao San Road' (418 m across).
notes: Famous backpacker street, lively at night.

text.description: Khaosan Road is a short, lively street in Bang Lamphu, laid out in 1892 and only about 410 m long. The name means milled rice, a nod to the area's older rice trade. Today it is known worldwide as a backpacker base, with guesthouses, market stalls, travel agents, bars and street food all packed into one stretch. That mix is why it photographs well: signs, stalls, food carts and people from all over the world fill every frame, and the mood changes a lot between day and night. The street was redone as a walking street in 2020, with vendors given allotted stalls, so the layout is tidier than older photos suggest. Just across from the road to the west stands Wat Chana Songkram, a centuries-old royal temple, which is a calm contrast if you want a quieter shot nearby. From the phone icon on the map you look south-east along the street towards its middle, so you can show its length, the crowd and the signs in one picture. Keep your phone close to your body in busy moments and take a few frames rather than waiting for a perfect one. Around 13-15 April, the Songkran water fights can fill the road, so protect your phone if you plan to take pictures then.
text.geographic_location: Khaosan Road is in the Bang Lamphu area of Phra Nakhon District, in central Bangkok, about 1 km north of the Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew. Wat Chana Songkram is directly opposite the road to the west.
text.directions_text: Check a local map app for the best route to the Bang Lamphu area, just north of the Grand Palace. If you start from the Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew, head north; it is about 1 km on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for natural street views. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the full width of the street, or to the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out signs and faces without stepping into the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Face south-east and look along the road towards the centre of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the road along a line so it leads the eye into the picture. Include signs and stalls in the foreground for depth. Try a telephoto shot (2x-5x) for a tighter, busier look. Hold the phone steady against your body or a wall for sharper night shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest sign to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so neon lights don't wash out. After dark, let night mode do its work and hold still for the full exposure. A Live Photo can catch people moving through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, once the bars and signs are lit, is the liveliest time for colour and atmosphere. Earlier in the day it is generally calmer and easier for clear, uncluttered views.

text.access_note: Khaosan Road is an open public street; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit during a special event such as Songkran.

name: Wat Pho
label: Wat Pho
camera_pill: near สวนมิสกวัน
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11169995: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Phra Chettuphon Wimon Mangkhalaram Ratchaworamahawihan' (495 m across).
notes: Home of the giant Reclining Buddha.

text.description:
Wat Pho is a large Buddhist temple complex on Rattanakosin Island, directly south of the Grand Palace. Most visitors know it as the Temple of the Reclining Buddha. The figure itself is 46 m (151 ft) long, and the grounds hold more than a thousand Buddha images, four great chedis (bell-shaped towers) and dozens of smaller ones. King Rama I rebuilt the temple from 1788 on an older site, and Rama III later enlarged it, so most of what you see today dates from that second big project. It is also known as the birthplace of traditional Thai massage, which is still taught here.

It photographs well because there is so much variety in one place. The chedis and rooflines suit wide, upward-looking shots. The courtyards and gate guardians, large stone figures that arrived as ballast on trading ships, make good close-up details. Rather than trying to get everything in one frame, plan a few different pictures: one wide view of the chedis, one detail of a guardian statue or roof edge, and one of the reclining Buddha if photography is allowed where you are standing.

The complex is big, with its large northern compound open to visitors, so allow time to wander. Keep your phone lens clean, as temple courtyards can be dusty, and step back from the walls so the rooflines are not cut off. Always check for signs about photography inside the halls.
text.geographic_location: Wat Pho is in Phra Nakhon District, on Rattanakosin Island in Bangkok. It sits directly south of the Grand Palace.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; use a map app to reach the Grand Palace area, then walk south. The Grand Palace is directly north of the temple. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m north-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for chedis, courtyards and the long reclining Buddha, then switch to the default lens (1x) for general views. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details and carved decoration that are out of reach.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Walk in towards it for closer shots of the buildings and chedis.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the chedis straight. Hold the phone level, and tilt up only a little so the towers do not lean. Leave some sky above the spires and include a foreground feature, such as a statue or a gateway, to give a sense of scale. Inside the long hall, shoot along the length of the figure rather than straight on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so that gold and white surfaces keep their detail. Use portrait mode for close-ups of statues, if the phone allows it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer and the courtyards are usually less crowded.

text.access_note: The northern compound is the part open to visitors, but this is an active temple, so check the official site before you go for entry rules, dress code and any photography limits indoors.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens helps fit the long reclining Buddha into a frame in a confined space.
Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and fewer people.
Photography may be restricted inside some halls, so look for signs.
Temple courtyards can be dusty, so the phone lens may need cleaning.
Rattanakosin Island visitors are likely to find the Grand Palace a useful starting point for walking to Wat Pho.

name: Baiyoke Tower II
label: Baiyoke Tower II
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q804055: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Tall hotel tower with a revolving rooftop observation deck.

text.description: Baiyoke Tower II is an 88-storey skyscraper hotel on Ratchaprarop Road. It stands 309 m tall, or 328.4 m with the antenna, which makes it the third tallest completed building in Bangkok. The Baiyoke Sky Hotel inside is the tallest hotel in Southeast Asia. Construction finished in 1997 and the antenna followed two years later. The tower is mostly a shape to photograph from the ground: a tall, slim, tapering building that fills the frame. Because you will be standing at its foot, you cannot fit the whole tower in a normal shot, so you have to decide whether to show the full height or just a section. Tilting the phone upwards makes the sides lean inwards, which can look dramatic if you do it on purpose. Shoot a few frames both ways and keep the one you prefer. If you want views from the building itself, there is a public observatory on the 77th floor and a revolving roof deck on the 84th floor. Check the official site before you go for current access arrangements.
text.geographic_location: In the Ratchathewi District of central Bangkok, at 222 Ratchaprarop Road. The tower rises well above the surrounding streets.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so head for the Ratchathewi District of Bangkok and Ratchaprarop Road by taxi or hired scooter. Ask for Baiyoke Tower II at 222 Ratchaprarop Road. The phone icon on the map is at the foot of the tower itself, so once you arrive there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because from the base you need the extra width to get a good amount of the tower into the frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less distorted view of the lower section. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the upper floors or the top of the tower against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back as far as is safe and comfortable to reduce how steeply the sides lean inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and line up one edge of the tower with a vertical gridline to keep it looking upright. Keep the phone as level as you can and leave a little sky above the top. For a bolder picture, tilt up with the ultra-wide (0.5x) and let the sides converge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not turn white. If the light is fading, switch on night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually works best, as the sky darkens. Try the same view again after dark with night mode.

text.access_note: The observatory and roof deck are inside the building, so check the official site before you go.

name: Lumphini Park
label: Lumphini Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'HI-SO' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'HI-SO Rooftop Bar' (node/7136730885): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23483299: large area 'Lumphini Park' (1203 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large central park with a lake and monitor lizards.

text.description:
Lumphini Park is a large green space in the middle of Bangkok's business district, and it works well for photos because it contrasts so strongly with the towers around it. It covers about 57.6 hectares (360 rai) and is regarded as the first public park in Bangkok. King Rama VI gave the land to the nation in 1925, and the park carries the name of Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace. The artificial lake, where visitors can hire boats, is the natural centre of most pictures. Around 400 Asian water monitors live in the park, so look for them on the paths and banks, and do not feed them.

From there the park is a block of trees and water spread out to the north, with the glass skyline all around it. At ground level the view across the lake, with high-rises showing through the trees, is the classic alternative. Wherever you stand, keep some foliage or water in the foreground so the city looks like it is rising out of the park. Check the horizon on your gridlines so the towers don't lean. Early morning and evening are the busiest times on the paths, which can add life to a shot.
text.geographic_location: Lumphini Park lies in the Lumphini sub-district of central Bangkok, on the north side of Rama IV Road between Ratchadamri Road and Witthayu Road.
text.directions_text: Head to SO Sofitel Bangkok at 2 North Sathon Road, close to the southern edge of the park near Rama IV Road, and take the lift to the 29th and 30th floors. If you want to walk in the park itself, Lumphini station on the Blue Line serves the corner where Witthayu and Rama IV roads meet. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the park and the skyline together. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out individual towers or the lake.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at HI-SO (29th and 30th floors of SO Sofitel Bangkok, 2 N Sathon Rd (rooftop bar, not a free deck)). A 360-degree elevated view of the park's greenery below and the glass skyline around it. It is a rooftop bar, not a free viewing deck, so check the official site before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the green of the park in the lower half of the frame and let the towers fill the top. Use the gridlines to keep the horizon level. Try a panorama for the full sweep, moving slowly and keeping your elbows tucked in. If you would rather be inside the park, the lake with the skyline above the trees is a good alternative, and so is the view across the pond near the Sepak Takraw Court.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the park to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone close to the glass or against a firm rail to cut reflections and shake. Use night mode after dark and hold still until it finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually works well, as the light softens and the city lights come on. Early morning is good if you are photographing the lake and joggers at ground level.

text.access_note: The park is a public space, but the rooftop bar HI-SO is a paid venue, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon into dusk usually gives soft light and lit-up buildings from a high viewpoint.
Windows or glass at a rooftop venue can cause reflections, and pressing the phone close to the glass reduces them.
Early morning and evening are the busiest times in the park, because of joggers.
Lifts take visitors up to the 29th and 30th floors of the hotel.

name: Wat Saket
label: Golden Mount
camera_pill: near ซอยบรมบรรพต
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Wat Saket'.
notes: Hilltop temple with a golden chedi and city views.

text.description:
Wat Saket is a Buddhist temple in Bangkok, and its best-known feature is Phu Khao Thong, the Golden Mountain. It is not a natural hill. King Rama III wanted a huge chedi (a bell-shaped Buddhist monument) on this spot, but Bangkok's soft ground could not carry the weight and the structure collapsed. Over the following decades the mud and brick took on the shape of a natural hill, overgrown with weeds, which locals simply called the mountain. A smaller chedi was later built on top and finished early in the reign of King Rama V. It was covered in gold and holds a relic of the Buddha brought from Sri Lanka. Concrete walls were added in the 1940s to stop the hill eroding.

That history is why it photographs so well. A steep artificial hill with a gold-covered chedi on top is an unusual shape, so the subject is easy to spot. It also works as a clear landmark picture to show where you have been. In November the chedi is wrapped in a long red cloth during the temple fair, which makes for a very different photo if you happen to be here then.

From the phone icon on the map the hill is a short walk away, so you can compose before you arrive. Keep the whole mound and the gold tip in one frame, and include a little foreground, such as a wall or a tree branch, to give a sense of scale. If you go up, be respectful of people praying and keep your phone low and quiet near worshippers.
text.geographic_location: Wat Saket is in the Pom Prap Sattru Phai district of Bangkok, just outside the old fortified part of the city. Phu Khao Thong, the Golden Mountain, stands inside the temple compound.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Pom Prap Sattru Phai district and go by taxi or hired scooter, asking for Wat Saket or the Golden Mountain. Walk east from there to reach the temple compound. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole hill and the sky above it. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the golden chedi on top. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the hill, the walls and the foreground in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Take a first photo from here, then walk towards the temple for closer views.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the chedi at the top-right or top-left crossing point rather than dead centre. Include a bit of tree, wall or rooftop at the bottom of the frame to show how steep and tall the hill is. Hold the phone upright for the full height of the hill. If you are closer to the base, use the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone level to stop the sides leaning inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gold chedi to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the gold keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. If you try a Live Photo, hold still for a moment after pressing the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the gold and fewer harsh shadows. Around the November temple fair, the red cloth on the chedi adds colour.

text.access_note: Wat Saket is a working place of worship, so dress modestly; check the official site before you go for entry rules and any charge for climbing the hill.

name: Wat Phra Kaew
label: Wat Phra Kaew
camera_source: Commons cluster (23 photos). Moved 73 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 10 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/230010054: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Phra Kaew' (223 m across).
notes: Temple of the Emerald Buddha inside the Grand Palace grounds.

text.description: Wat Phra Kaew, the Temple of the Emerald Buddha, is regarded as the most sacred Buddhist temple in Thailand. It sits inside the Grand Palace in the historical centre of Bangkok. It photographs well because it is a cluster of buildings rather than a single one. Gold-leaf pavilions, tall spires and roofs of blue, yellow and orange glazed tiles sit close together, so there is something new to frame every few steps. Building began in 1783 under Rama I, the first king of the Chakri dynasty, and later kings have kept adding to and restoring it. The Emerald Buddha was moved here in 1785 from Wat Arun across the river. The ordination hall, the Ubosot, is one of the oldest structures here. It is ringed by a low wall with eight small pavilions, each holding a gold-covered boundary stone. For a phone, the colour and detail do most of the work. Start with a wide shot to show how the buildings crowd together, then move in on the roof edges, spires and gilded details. Take a few shots at different zoom levels from the same spot, because the courtyards can be busy and you may not be able to step back or sideways easily. Keep the phone straight and use gridlines to stop the tall spires leaning.
text.geographic_location: In the historical centre of Bangkok, on Rattanakosin Island, in the north-eastern corner of the Outer Court of the Grand Palace, on the east bank of the Chao Phraya River.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Start from the Grand Palace area on Rattanakosin Island and follow the visitor route inside the grounds. The temple lies within the Grand Palace grounds. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the spires and rooflines into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for general views, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof ends, pediments and gold details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on ถนนสนามไชย (Sanam Chai Road) (grassy area outside the palace wall, looking west). A wide panorama of the whole Wat Phra Kaew complex, with the ubosot on the right and the spires of the main buildings in a row. Face west and photograph the buildings in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight so the spires do not lean. Use the ultra-wide for a scene-setting shot, then zoom in on the tiled roofs and gilded details. Tap the brightest roof or the gold surface to focus, and lower the exposure slider slightly so the gold keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the gold surfaces, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the highlights do not blow out. Use a Live Photo if people are moving through the scene, so you can pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer and the light is softer. Midday sun can make the gold and tiles glare, so lower the exposure then.

text.access_note: This is a royal temple and a place of worship inside the Grand Palace and is open to visitors on most days, but check the official site before you go for tickets, opening times and dress rules.

name: Yaowarat Road
label: Yaowarat Chinatown
camera_pill: near ถนนมังกร
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/16815834: large area 'Yaowarat Road' (1448 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Main street of Chinatown, famous for neon signs and street food.

text.description:
Yaowarat Road is the main street of Bangkok's Chinatown, and it is at its most photogenic when the area turns into a street of food stalls and shopfronts in the evening. The road is about 1.5 km long and 20 m wide. It was built between 1892 and 1900 under King Rama V, on land that had been rice fields and canals. Its name means "young king" and honours Prince Vajirunhis, the first crown prince of Thailand. The road is also known as the "Dragon Road" because its curving line is said to resemble a dragon's body, and as the "Golden Road" for its many gold shops.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the layers of street life: shop signs stacked above the pavement, people walking, and the food stalls that draw both tourists and locals. During Chinese New Year the road is closed to traffic and becomes a pedestrian street. That is a good time for wide, open views, though it will be busy.

The subject is a point along this long road. Take a few frames in each direction, since there is something to shoot every few steps. Keep your phone close to your body in crowds, and stay on the pavement when you stop to shoot.
text.geographic_location: Yaowarat Road is in Samphanthawong District, at the heart of Bangkok's Chinatown. It runs parallel to Charoen Krung Road, in the Chinatown area bordered by the Chao Phraya River, close to Phahurat (Little India).
text.directions_text: Wat Mangkon Station on the MRT Blue Line serves the road, so you can start there and walk towards Yaowarat. The road is also served by several bus lines, with four bus stops along it. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for street scenes that look the way you saw them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit tall signs and a narrow pavement into one frame. Use 2x or more for details such as a food stall or a single sign.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edge of the road or the row of shopfronts with a grid line, so the street leads into the picture. Include a sign or a person in the foreground for depth. Take a wide frame first, then a closer one of a single stall or sign.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright sign to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights keep their colour. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall for a second or two.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the road turns into a food street and the signs are lit. Earlier in the day is quieter and easier for wide shots.

text.access_note: Yaowarat Road is an open public street, but it is busy with traffic and people; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit during Chinese New Year or to enter any shop or shrine.

name: MahaNakhon
label: MahaNakhon Skywalk
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/444651219: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '' (120 m across).
notes: Pixelated skyscraper with a rooftop glass-floor viewing deck.

text.description:
MahaNakhon, now called King Power Mahanakhon, is a glass tower in Bangkok's Silom and Sathon business district. It stands 314.2 metres tall with 77 floors, and when it was recognised as complete in 2016 it was the tallest building in Thailand. A newer tower has since overtaken it. The name Mahanakhon is part of Bangkok's ceremonial name and means "great city".

It photographs well because it doesn't look like a plain box. A ribbon of stepped, cube-shaped cut-outs spirals up one side and peels back the outer glass skin. This gives the tower a pixelated, slightly unfinished look and creates balconies along the way. The German architect Ole Scheeren was part of the design team. Those stepped edges give you strong diagonal lines and a lot of texture, even on a hazy day.

The tower is very tall, so your main challenge is fitting it into the frame. From the phone icon on the map, you are right at its foot. Tilt the phone up and let the spiral lead the eye to the sky. For a view of the whole tower, step back along the pavement and use a wider shot. The building also holds a hotel, residences and a rooftop observation deck, but access and what is open can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the Silom/Sathon central business district of Bangkok, among the office towers and busy roads of the city's commercial centre.
text.directions_text: Head for the Silom and Sathon business district and look for King Power Mahanakhon, formerly MahaNakhon. It is a very tall tower in the district. Once you are at the base, the phone icon on the map is right at the foot of the tower. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the spiral and a good slice of sky into one shot. Then switch to the default lens (1x) from further back, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the stepped cut-outs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you will be pointing the phone steeply upwards. For a gentler, fuller view of the whole tower, walk a little way back along the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line one edge of the tower up with a vertical grid line. Looking up makes the sides lean inwards, which can look dramatic. If you want straighter sides, step back and shoot from lower down. Let the spiral of cut-outs run diagonally through the frame, and include a little sky for breathing space. For a detail shot, use telephoto on the pixelated pattern of the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the glass doesn't wash out. At dusk, use night mode and rest your elbows against a wall or railing to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening, when the glass picks up warm light and then the blue of dusk. Take care with strong midday sun, which can cause glare on the glass.

text.access_note: The area around the tower is a busy city streetscape, but the tower contains a hotel, residences and an observation deck, so check the official site before you go for what is open to visitors.
claims_not_in_sources: The glass picks up warm light in the late afternoon and blue tones at dusk.
Strong midday sun can cause glare on the glass.
Standing at the base and pointing the phone upwards makes the tower's sides appear to lean inwards.
A newer tower has overtaken it as the tallest in Thailand (the sources say this happened in 2018, but not what the current record holder is).

name: Giant Swing
label: Giant Swing
camera_source: Commons cluster (21 photos). Moved 59 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 160 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/178353988: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Giant Swing' (15 m across).
notes: Red teak swing frame in front of Wat Suthat.

text.description:
The Giant Swing, known in Thai as Sao Chingcha, is a tall red teak frame standing in front of Wat Suthat in Phra Nakhon, the old part of Bangkok. It is 21.15 m tall and was first built in 1784 under King Rama I. It was once used in a Brahmin swinging ceremony, which stopped in 1935 after several fatal accidents. The present timbers date from a major rebuild in 2005-2007, when six teak trunks were used. The original timbers are kept in the Bangkok National Museum.

It photographs well because the shape is so simple. Two tall posts and a crossbar make a bold, easy-to-read outline, and the temple and shrine buildings around it give you colour and context. You can step closer for a tighter shot.

The swing stands directly in front of the Devasathan, the Royal Brahmin Office, and close to Wat Suthat. A once-a-year sunset alignment, when the sun sets in the middle of the swing, usually falls in early March; it fell on 6 March in 2025. If you are there on a normal day, keep an eye on traffic and other visitors, and shoot the swing as a whole rather than waiting for a perfectly empty street.
text.geographic_location: In the Sao Chingcha Subdistrict of Phra Nakhon District, in the old part of Bangkok. It stands in front of Wat Suthat and the Devasathan, close to the City Hall and the Lan Kon Mueang open square.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole swing with its surroundings. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the posts closer from where you stand. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk right up to the base.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Wat Suthat Thepwararam Ratchaworamahawihan (steps of the temple, directly opposite the swing across Bamrung Mueang Road). The whole swing framed by the temple's stone gateway, shot from above the road so that vehicles are mostly kept out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the swing's centre line on the middle vertical line, so the two posts look balanced. Keep the top crossbar clear of the screen edge with a little sky above it. A zoomed shot from here compresses the swing against the buildings behind it. A wide shot from nearer the base shows its height.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red posts to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the colour stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone with both hands when zoomed, as small movements show more.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the red timber.

text.access_note: The swing is in front of Wat Suthat and the Devasathan, which are places of worship, so check the official sites before you go if you plan to go inside either.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the red timber.
The best spot to see the early-March sunset alignment may be different from the stand-here point.
Traffic and other visitors may be around the swing.

name: Jim Thompson House
label: Jim Thompson House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jim Thompson House' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/341577338: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jim Thompson House' (102 m across).
notes: Traditional Thai teak house museum in a garden.

text.description:
Jim Thompson House is a small compound of traditional Thai teak houses, set in a tropical garden in the middle of Bangkok. It was built in 1959 as the home of Jim Thompson, the American businessman who founded the Thai Silk Company and collected Southeast Asian art. The land is only about one rai (roughly half an acre), so everything sits close together. The six houses stand on stilts. Most of them are 19th-century buildings that were taken down in Ayutthaya and re-erected here, and the largest, a weaver's house, came from the Bangkrua community across the canal. The site sits beside the Saen Saep canal.

It photographs well because the dark wood, steep roofs and green planting make a ready-made frame. The phone icon on the map is at the house itself, so you shoot from the garden and courtyard walkways outside the teak houses. From there you can see the houses on their stilts, framed by the trees. Look for the main courtyard staircase, the riverside pavilion and the garden corners. Photography outside is welcome, but the rules for the interior are not clear, and the interior is visited on a guided tour only. Ask at the entrance before you take your phone out indoors, and never use flash. For a different view, try the canal side, where you can see the red teak façade from Saphan Hua Chang. The Ban Krua side of the canal may also give a quieter view back toward the compound.
text.geographic_location: The house is in Pathumwan, central Bangkok, at Soi Kasemsan 2 off Rama I Road, one block from the National Stadium. The house sits beside the Saen Saep canal.
text.directions_text: Take the BTS to National Stadium and leave by exit 1. The house is about five minutes on foot from there, down Soi Kasemsan 2, which runs off Rama I Road. Follow the signs for the museum entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of the houses. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in tight spots such as the courtyard and the foot of the staircase. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof ends, carved details and the far side of the garden.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Jim Thompson House's garden and courtyard walkways, outside the teak houses. From there the photo shows the six stilted teak houses framed by the tropical garden and the trees around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the stilts and roof edges with them, so the houses do not lean. Use a leafy branch or the courtyard staircase as a foreground frame. Take one wide shot of the whole group, then step closer for details. If you want a different angle, the canal side offers views of the red teak façade from Saphan Hua Chang, and the Ban Krua side of the canal may give a quieter view back toward the compound.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dark teak to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright sky and sunlit leaves do not wash out. Portrait mode works for people on the walkways but can blur the carved edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning, when it is cooler and calmer and the garden light is better before the midday glare.

text.access_note: The interior is visited on a guided tour, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Photography indoors may be restricted, so ask staff at the entrance before taking photos inside.
Strong midday sun may make contrast between sunlit leaves and dark teak harder for a phone to handle.
Portrait mode may blur fine carved edges.
The Ban Krua side of the canal may give a quieter view back toward the compound.

name: Wat Traimit
label: Golden Buddha
camera_source: Commons cluster (71 photos). Moved 65 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 40 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/241879483: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Traimit Witthayaram Worawihan' (213 m across).
notes: Temple housing a solid gold Buddha statue.

text.description: Wat Traimit is a Buddhist temple in Bangkok's Chinatown (Samphanthawong district), best known for the solid-gold Buddha statue kept in its tall marble pavilion, the Phra Maha Mondop. The pavilion is four storeys high, finished in marble, with a gilded multi-tiered roof and spire, so it gives a bright, clean subject against the busy streets around it. The story behind the statue adds interest to your photos. It was covered in plaster and moved here in 1935. In 1955 it was accidentally dropped during a move, the plaster cracked, and the gold underneath was revealed. The Mondop was completed in 2007 and opened to the public in February 2010. The top floor holds the Golden Buddha, and the lower floors have exhibitions, including the Yaowarat Chinatown Heritage Center. The temple grounds also have the 1947 ordination hall (ubosot) and the monks' quarters from 1937. Both received a conservation award in 2011. For a phone photo, the pavilion is the obvious main subject, and the ornate roofline is the part that stands out most. Look for a clear gap between other visitors and the building, and keep the vertical lines straight with the gridlines. Take a wide shot first, then move closer for the gold detail. Inside, areas may have their own photography rules, so follow any signs and check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Wat Traimit is in Samphanthawong district, in the Chinatown (Yaowarat) area of Bangkok. The temple grounds are about 213 m across.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Yaowarat Chinatown area of Samphanthawong district and ask for Wat Traimit, by taxi or hired scooter. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pavilion and its surroundings. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the whole building in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the gilded roof and spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Phra Maha Mondop (front of the building, at the foot of the main staircase where the steps begin). The white marble, gold-trimmed four-storey building and its front staircase, framed straight on from the bottom of the steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the pavilion's vertical edges with them so the building does not lean. Leave a little sky above the spire. Then zoom in to 2x or more for a second shot of the gilded roof. Try not to tilt the phone upwards too much, because the walls will look as if they are falling backwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the marble walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the gold and white keep their detail. Take a few shots, since people will often walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the gold and marble, and fewer tour groups than midday.

text.access_note: This is an active Buddhist temple and visitor attraction, so rules on access, dress and photography inside may apply; check the official site before you go.

name: Erawan Shrine
label: Erawan Shrine
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Erawan Shrine' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/373104218: the OpenStreetMap point 'Erawan Shrine'.
notes: Busy Brahma shrine at the Ratchaprasong intersection.

text.description:
The Erawan Shrine, formally the Thao Maha Phrom Shrine, is a shrine at the Ratchaprasong intersection in central Bangkok. It holds a gilded statue of Phra Phrom, the Thai form of the Hindu god Brahma, shown with four faces. It is worshipped by many people outside a strictly Hindu setting, and the shrine mixes Hindu and Buddhist ideas. It was built in 1956 beside the old Erawan Hotel, and the statue was enshrined on 9 November 1956. After the statue was destroyed in 2006, an identical one was placed here in May of that year.

It photographs well because everything happens at close range. The gold faces, the flower garlands and offerings, and the colour of the crowd all sit within a few metres of each other. Thai dance troupes are sometimes hired by worshippers to perform here, which can add movement to a shot. Lighting incense and candles has not been allowed since March 2020.

For a clean frontal shot, stand at the front on the southeast side of the statue and keep a little distance. Crowds tend to block the view less from this side. Keep out of the way of people who are praying, do not use flash, and do not step onto the shrine base. For an overhead view of the roof and the crowd, the Chit Lom Station walkway and nearby shopping malls look down on the shrine.
text.geographic_location: The shrine is in Lumphini Subdistrict, Pathum Wan District, at the Ratchaprasong intersection on Ratchadamri Road. It sits next to the Grand Hyatt Erawan Bangkok, with malls such as Gaysorn, CentralWorld and Amarin Plaza close by.
text.directions_text: The easiest landmark is Chit Lom Station on the BTS Skytrain, which has an elevated walkway overlooking the shrine. Walk down from the walkway to street level at the Ratchaprasong intersection and the shrine is near the Grand Hyatt Erawan Bangkok. If you come by taxi, ask for the Erawan Shrine at Ratchaprasong. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main shot. It gives a natural, clean frontal view of the statue without stretching the edges. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole shrine and crowd, and keep people away from the frame edges, where they look distorted. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for details of the faces and offerings without pointing the phone at worshippers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you get a close, clear view of the gilded four-faced Brahma image, with offerings and flowers in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep a little distance and shoot straight on, so the four-faced image fills the middle of the frame. Turn on the gridlines and put the statue on the central line, with flowers along the bottom. Wait for a gap in the crowd instead of leaning over people. For a different view, the Ratchaprasong Skywalk and CentralWorld give an overhead look at the shrine's roof and the busy junction.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the gold keeps its detail instead of turning pale. Turn the flash off. Try a Live Photo to catch a dance performance or drifting garlands, but hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mid-morning, when light falls evenly on the faces, or early morning (about 06:00-09:00) for softer light and fewer people.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so dress and behave respectfully, and check the official site before you go for current opening times and any rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Visitors to a place of worship in Thailand are generally expected to dress modestly and behave respectfully.
The walkway from Chit Lom Station leads down to street level close to the shrine.
Tapping to focus and lowering exposure helps keep detail in bright gold surfaces on a phone.
The ultra-wide lens can distort people near the edges of the frame.
Overhead viewpoints at the skywalk and CentralWorld are only reachable at mall or walkway opening times.

name: Wat Suthat
label: Wat Suthat
camera_pill: near ถนนบำรุงเมือง
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/32011053: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wat Suthat Thep Wararam Ratchaworamahawihan' (382 m across).
notes: Royal temple with a huge viharn and a Buddha statue.

text.description: Wat Suthat is a first-class royal temple in the Inner Rattanakosin area of old Bangkok. King Rama I began it in 1807. Rama II helped carve the wooden doors of the main hall, and it was finished in the reign of Rama III, around 1847. Its great bronze Buddha, Phra Si Sakyamuni, is about eight metres high and was brought from Sukhothai. The ordination hall (ubosot) is regarded as the longest in Thailand, and the doors and windows are topped with small spired pediments that look good in close-up. Around the lower terrace of the main base stand twenty-eight Chinese pagodas, each standing for one of the twenty-eight Buddhas of the Theravada tradition. The Giant Swing stands directly in front of the temple, which makes a good second subject. The temple photographs well because of its scale, its repeated rooflines and the cloister walls with their carved boundary-stone shrines. From the phone icon on the map, look south and take a wide first shot to show how the buildings sit together. Then move closer for details: roof edges, doorways, the pagodas and the shrine pairs along the wall. Inside the halls, expect dim light and be ready for people sitting or praying; take photos quietly and keep the camera away from worshippers' faces.
text.geographic_location: Wat Suthat is in the Inner Rattanakosin area of old Bangkok, and the Giant Swing stands directly in front of it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Inner Rattanakosin area of old Bangkok and ask for Wat Suthat or the Giant Swing. From the phone icon on the map it is about 2 minutes on foot to the middle of the temple grounds, which lie to the south. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m north of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the buildings as you see them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long cloister walls and rooflines, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details, spires and carvings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m north of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Take your first shot from here, then walk in for closer details.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizontal roof and wall lines level, because the buildings have strong repeating shapes. Use a doorway or gap in the wall as a frame, and wait for a monk or visitor to walk through for scale. For a shot of the long ordination hall, use ultra-wide from the side and hold the phone level so the walls don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of a gilded or white surface and slide the exposure down a little so the gold and white keep their detail. Indoors, hold the phone steady with both hands and let night mode help if the app offers it. Check whether photography is allowed inside before you take any pictures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning if you can, when there are fewer people and the light is softer. Midday sun is harsh on the bright surfaces.

text.access_note: Wat Suthat is a working Buddhist temple and a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for current access rules and visiting conditions.

name: Democracy Monument
label: Democracy Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ถนนดินสอ' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of ถนนดินสอ and ถนนราชดำเนินกลาง (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/178329973: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Democracy Monument' (82 m across).
notes: Art Deco monument on Ratchadamnoen Avenue.

text.description: Democracy Monument stands in the middle of a traffic circle on Ratchadamnoen Avenue, the wide boulevard running through Bangkok's old city centre. Four tall, wing-like structures surround a central turret, and the whole thing is built on a bold, symmetrical plan. That makes it easy to read in a photo, even from the pavement. It was commissioned in 1939 to mark the 1932 change to a constitutional monarchy. The four wings are 24 metres high and stand for the army, navy, air force and police. On top, a carved palm-leaf manuscript box holds the 1932 constitution. The relief sculptures around the base were carried out by the Italian-born sculptor Corrado Feroci, who later took the Thai name Silpa Bhirasi. Traffic here is heavy, and the island is hard to reach on foot when it is busy, so photograph from the pavement and stay off the crossings. If you want a straighter, more symmetrical view of the four wings and the tower, or a clean wide shot with the tree-lined boulevard behind, those are the two other viewpoints worth trying. Take a few frames with different amounts of sky and road, and check the result before you move on.
text.geographic_location: In the city centre of Bangkok, on a traffic circle where Ratchadamnoen Avenue meets Dinso Road. It sits roughly halfway between Sanam Luang and the Golden Mount (Phu Kao Thong).
text.directions_text: There is no nearby station or tram stop at this spot. The monument sits roughly halfway between Sanam Luang and the Golden Mount, so use either area as your reference point. Look for Democracy Monument (Anusawari Prachathipatai) on Ratchadamnoen Avenue. A new MRT station next to the monument is under construction, so expect some pavement disruption. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the base, the wings and some of the boulevard into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view, and use the telephoto (2x or more) only for details such as the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of ถนนดินสอ and ถนนราชดำเนินกลาง (corner where Dinso Road meets Ratchadamnoen Klang Road). A wide-angle view of the monument's base and wings set against the boulevard and surrounding traffic. For a straight-on, symmetrical view of the four wings and the central tower, try the monument itself (อนุสาวรีย์ประชาธิปไตย).
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower on the vertical line so the wings look even. Leave a little road in the foreground to show the size of the circle. For a cleaner shot with the tree line behind, try ถนนราชดำเนินกลาง. Stay on the pavement and off the pedestrian crossings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the monument to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the wings keep their detail. In heavy traffic, try a Live Photo and pick the frame with the fewest vehicles.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day and take a test shot.

text.access_note: The monument is a public landmark on a busy road, and the traffic island is hard to reach on foot when traffic is heavy. Photograph from the pavement, stay off the crossings, and check the official site or local notices for roadworks before you go.

name: Asiatique The Riverfront
label: Asiatique
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Asiatique Sky' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Asiatique Sky Ferris Wheel' (way/342522015): middle (54 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
notes: Riverside night market with a Ferris wheel.

text.description:
Asiatique is a large open-air riverside market and dining complex on the Chao Phraya River, built on the old docks of the Danish-owned East Asiatic Company. The company owned port facilities here, which closed in 1947, and the oldest surviving warehouse dates from 1907. Many of the warehouses now hold shops and restaurants, and the complex opened in its present form on 27 April 2012. That mix of old warehouses and bright modern lighting gives you plenty to point a phone at.

The best-known photo subject is Asiatique Sky, the Ferris wheel. At 60 metres it is the tallest in Bangkok, and it stands right beside the water. Stand at its base and the steel wheel rises against the sky, with the river and the city lights behind it as the sun goes down. Other things to look for are the 300-metre riverside promenade, the tall-ship restaurant Sirimahannop (a replica of a merchant barque) and the double-deck carousel with its fairytale look, which sits close enough to the wheel to share a frame with it.

For the wheel, arrive about an hour before sunset. You get warm light first, then the wheel's lights and the city coming on. Photographing from the ground beside the wheel is free, but riding it needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go if you want shots from the top.
text.geographic_location: Asiatique is in Bang Kho Laem District in Bangkok. It faces the Chao Phraya River and backs on to Charoen Krung Road.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed nearby. Access is by road, with a car park on site, or by boat: a shuttle runs from Sathon Pier. Once inside, head for the Ferris wheel on the riverside. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the base of the wheel, because it is tall and close. Use the default lens (1x) from a few steps back for a tidier, less stretched view with the sky around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (west side of the wheel, at the base near the wheel entrance). The steel wheel rising against the sky, with the river and city lights behind it as the sun sets. The main part of the complex lies a short walk to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the wheel's central post up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Keep the wheel on one side and leave the river and lights on the other. For a different view, walk along the riverside walkway and turn round to shoot the Bangkok skyline and river behind you. You can also frame the double-deck carousel with the wheel rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wheel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights stay colourful and the sky does not turn white. Once it is properly dark, switch to night mode and brace your elbows against a railing or your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive about an hour before sunset. Take your wide shots in the warm light, then stay on for the lit wheel and city lights.

text.access_note: The complex is an open-air shopping and dining area, and you can photograph the wheel from the ground for free, but riding Asiatique Sky is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing close to the base of a 60-metre wheel, the whole wheel is hard to fit in the default lens (1x), so the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps.

text.description:
Lebua at State Tower is a luxury hotel on Silom Road, right beside the Chao Phraya River in Bang Rak. For a phone photographer the appeal is its height. The tower stands well above the surrounding streets, and a cluster of restaurants and bars called The Dome by lebua sits at the very top. The rooftop restaurant Sirocco and the Sky Bar are both on the 64th floor. Since New Year's Eve 2015, Sirocco has hosted what is described as the highest New Year's Eve ball drop in the world. That makes the building easy to recognise from far away, and a good subject from the street too.

The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, so you are photographing the building from its foot. Tilt your phone upwards and use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit more of the height into the frame. Use the gridlines to keep the vertical edges as straight as you can; this works best if you hold the phone level and then raise it a little, rather than tipping it far back. If you want a closer detail of the upper floors, the telephoto lens (2x-5x) will pick out the top of the tower. Dusk is a good time to come, when the building starts to light up against the sky. Check the official site before you go if you plan to go up to the bars or restaurants.
text.geographic_location: Lebua at State Tower is on Silom Road in the Bang Rak District of Bangkok, beside the Chao Phraya River.
text.directions_text: Start from Silom Road in Bang Rak and go by taxi or hired scooter to the tower, next to the Chao Phraya River. The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, so there is no extra walk once you arrive. Ask your driver for "lebua at State Tower" and you will be dropped at the foot of the building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the tall tower into the frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the lower floors, and to the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details near the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the tower rises straight above you, so you will be shooting upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's vertical edges up with them. Tilt the phone up only as far as you need, because a steep tilt makes the sides lean inwards. Put a strip of sky or a tree or lamp at the edge of the frame to give the height some scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky is not washed out and the tower keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and brace your arms against your body or a solid surface to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk, when the sky still has some colour and the building's lights are coming on, is a good time to try.

text.access_note: The tower is a hotel with restaurants and bars on the upper floors, so access to them may be restricted or ticketed; check the official site before you go.
